cards.body: I think people often misunderstand ADHD and autism and spectrums and binaries and things like that.
A cluster of characteristics. [[One word for a bundle of traits that tend to travel together.]]
Reduced theory of mind — what makes it a disorder?
Honk. Sensory sensitivity.
Good at counting, number tricks. Savant status.
Binary: autistic. I am this — autistic, and not autistic.
Autistic people, not autistic people. I am autistic. Oh, wait a second. Maybe it's a spectrum.
And then — oh, wait, maybe it's just a cluster. A spectrum versus a cluster.
Actually, it's just the genes. Once you realize, then you'll never see it the same. Double helix.
I didn't say it was just one gene. It is just genes. We tried to simplify our genes, to no success. But that's okay — it was still worth the question mark.
[[Draw autistic and non-autistic as two hills — they overlap in the middle, with no clean line.]]

Autism, ADHD, math genius — I'm not sure what that says. ADHD, sensory sensitivity: they have that in common. Clutter, time management. Always counting. Obsessive — OCD. Outbursts, crying — bipolar disorder. Hmm?

cards.h: But wait — what’s with everyone on TikTok?
cards.body: So now we know. But wait. What's with everyone on TikTok saying everything is autism, ADHD? Do you pick your nose? Then you might have ADHD. Oh no.

cards.h: The reality is that it’s genes
cards.body: We tried to reduce something that is actually pretty complicated, and we kept making it more and more complicated. And the reality is that it's genes.
Some people obviously have the gender one — or people assume that they're going to perform similarly to their gender, but they don't.
Basically, it's the idea that dysphoria is not just gendered, and it can be about anything.

For example, I'm often misaged. That's not a word, but people think I'm really young because I'm short. I might have sort of a baby face. I'm, like, four eleven, but I'm thirty-four, and people think I'm twenty-two. And I always don't get respected. It's very annoying.
That's just one example. Everyone has different ones. [[Capable, in charge, and still handed the coffee cup and talked over.]]
[[Gender is a single guess in a whole cluster people pin on you at a glance.]]
[[In seconds, they’ve placed you on their own mental charts. You are here.]]
[[A vague shape, then a sharper guess, then the closest they’ll ever come. Never exactly you.]]
A girl with a snake coming out of her body. It feels like she has something inside her that is not being recognized.
Or an alien that's unzipping her own human face mask. I think I've seen that image before.
The lesson is about extracting and extrapolating from that concept, and realizing that it's not just one thing.
It's sort of similar to genes: like, being gay versus being straight, in some sort of square with thinking you're a boy versus feeling like a girl. People get confused about that.

cards.h: [[Who you want, and who you are]]
cards.body: [[One line is who you are drawn to. The other is who you are. They cross, and each one moves on its own.]]
[[Attraction runs across a range, end to end. Gender runs across a range too. Steps, not a switch.]]

I don't know what the exact percentages are, but most people probably are straight and think they're the same gender that they are. And maybe it's ten percent the otherwise. But any combination is possible.
[[Knowing who a person loves tells you nothing about whether they feel like a man or a woman. The two never line up on their own.]]

cards.h: Discovering their masculine and feminine side
cards.body: Let's do one where someone's discovering their masculine and feminine side. [[Part of it is inherited — a lean set early. The rest a whole life shapes.]]
[[Who you want, and who you are. Each of them a range. Every mix is a real person on the grid.]]

My uncle Corey visited, and explained everything to me in terms of himself — like, his family dynamics. His dad expected too much of him, because he was given a lot of responsibility when he was young: he gave him a paper route, and he lost the list of newspapers, because most people were twelve and he was ten. As I was listening, I understood what he was saying — but I also kind of saw it as something a therapist would say to him, to help him understand things from a perspective.

You have certain thoughts that are getting you from one place to the other. And you need them — basically believing things that aren't even true sometimes, just because they help you move on with your day.
There is nothing wrong with that. And I think it's beneficial to paint ourselves as the hero sometimes, if we're having trouble painting ourselves as the villain — or the victim.

A girl giving herself positive affirmations in the mirror — pointing at herself, standing in front of a long oval mirror, smiling and saying, like, I am beautiful. I'm strong. That's an inside thought: she can't just say that to other people and they have to believe her.
[[People who can’t tell themselves a generous story at all tend to be more depressed, not wiser.]]

cards.h: That’s not how I talk to myself
cards.body: I was talking to my ex-boyfriend on the phone, and I said something like, I'm an ungrateful bitch — in reference to my mom. And he said, oh, you should go to therapy, cause that's negative self-talk. And I was like, yeah, but that's not how I talk to myself. To myself I would say: it's hard for me that she doesn't understand.
However, it's important to be aware that these are inside thoughts. Private — keep out.

cards.h: Which are for others, which are for you
cards.body: The self-aware version of this is knowing which thoughts are for others and which ones are for you. Sort of like public and private thoughts.

I went on this date with this guy who was, like, five-eight — and remember, I'm really small too. And I told him: it's not that he's too short. It's that he can like his height personally, but still not like how it relates to people in the world — because people do have that bias. It's about accepting the accuracy of this disconnect. Allowing the fact that the inside and outside don't have to match — because it gives you so much more leeway. You can think one thing, and the world can think another.
It reminds me of my aunt deciding that she wants to be called Parvati suddenly, because she got in touch with her spiritual side. I think the point here is this sort of interesting disconnect.

cards.h: Doing the work, or forcing the world
cards.body: There's a more uncomfortable and deeper thread here, about doing self-discovery work and digging in, like shadow work — realizing, oh, I actually have masculine and feminine parts to myself — versus forcing people to call you by a different name and getting mad at them anytime they accidentally slip up.

[[He was always talking shit about people. Clearly cognitive vehicles — he could have that feeling of protection for himself without projecting it onto the world as fact. Kept inside, it’s armor. Handed out as truth, it’s just contempt.]]
[[And with no kind story to ride, shame floods in and you get stuck in the dip.]]
I think, actually, it might be better called inside and outside thoughts. [[Keep the vehicles — and know which is which.]]

This is called the metaphor machine, and it's basically how I think about art. It's kind of like this giant machine — but it's actually in our heads. In order for this to work, it's helpful to visualize it as a real machine.

The abstraction can exist without the thing. It exists in, like, an abstract plane — sort of like whatever that guy with the cave described. Plato, and the chairs, you know? They all have something in common.
It's part of the difference between a kit and a set. Like, a tea set: each of the pieces is different, but they all have something that is in common — like, they all have little nice flowers on them.

Versus, like, a doctor's kit, or a first-aid kit. None of the pieces have anything in common, but they all have a common purpose of healing you when you're sick. Band-Aids, and those weird little hammer things that knock on your knee — they don't have anything in common with each other specifically, but they all have a purpose.

cards.h: Two ways of dealing with abstraction
cards.body: It's sort of two ways of dealing with abstraction. One is that everything has the same thing in common — that's the pattern, the repetition. And the other is, like, a description.

Rather than deciding whether something's good or bad, you have a metaphor. You say, like, oh, your art piece is like this. And then: no, actually, it's like this. In one version, the metaphors are each describing a piece of it — getting closer and closer to the actual thing. Or another version is that each metaphor has something in common with it, and that thing in common describes it. Like, a cherry, because it's red. And then a sun, cause it's hot. Et cetera, et cetera.

How it works is there's almost like a conveyor belt, and into it goes raw materials — things in the real world. Things people say, or books, or art pieces. Or just moments. And then these go into the machine, and they get transformed into abstraction.

This brings you back to patterns — this idea I've had forever, about collecting patterns, almost like a religious activity. Like putting on tefillin: you tie these matchboxes all over your body, onto your arms and legs and hands and feet. Any time you see an example of something in the world that looks like that pattern, you put it into your box.

cards.h: The way our brains actually work
cards.body: Of course, this is mimicking the way that our brains actually work. It's a bit like the times-I idea, you know — oh, times I was brave. Oh, there's another time I was brave. Or, like, times someone was listening to me and then they just started looking at their phone. Okay, that's another one.

cards.h: The same relationship a soul has to a body
cards.body: In the center, this little weird device thing sort of spins them around, and basically discards the physical aspect of them. And what's left is the abstraction that was inside. It has sort of the same relationship that a soul has to a body. It's the essence.

Your brain just automatically strips it of patterns, and then constructs those into an abstract concept of what they're referring to. [[That is what every one of these lessons is doing to you right now.]]

I was thinking about Mason, who has reddish hair, kind of like a Viking. He's, like, a poet philosopher. Beard, longish hair, shoulder length. Basically thinking about how he makes art — but I want to call it, like, noise art, which is actually a genre of music. Basically, it's this process of taking an input, and then changing it, and then seeing the result, and then changing that, and then blah, blah, blah.

cards.h: Your brain can tell it’s not random
cards.body: What you get is basically something that looks like art — because it's as complicated, because it's been through various, you know, thingies. So your brain can tell it's not random. And it just assumes there's — it assumes it means something.

cards.h: It kind of blocks it up
cards.body: So it goes through the metaphor machine. And it kind of blocks it up — because it doesn't mean anything. But it does pass through all the gates.

The gates might be like: is it complicated enough? Are there patterns? Is there, like, a juxtaposition of ideas? Basically, all are hints that there's a meaning — but you can't actually know if there's a meaning until you feed it through the machine. You can imagine almost, like, a bouncer standing in front of a nightclub, checking ID: okay, do you have any of these three to five signs that often refer to abstraction? ([[The gates are their own lesson.]])

Patterns are really helpful, but there's two kinds of patterns. One describes the thing. One describes the creator of the thing, and talks about their intentionality — makes it clear that they were intentional in their pursuit.

There's two things we can extrapolate from this — someone pulling apart beef jerky, to show that it needs to be disentangled. One thing that becomes two. There's two things: one is the interesting part, and one is the boring part.

The metaphor for the boring part is giving someone something to do that's yours. Like dumping a pile of work — like Miriam's coworker, who did therapy, and dumped a bunch of work into her arms and said, my therapist says I'm not supposed to take on any more work. Basically giving someone a job that's not really theirs. Because the question is: who is the artist in this case? Is it the person who interprets all this noise?

You take a random pattern of dots, and you find meaning in it. Like a teacup with tea grounds at the bottom — the before and after. The before is just the grounds; they're clumping into little shapes, let's say. And then the after-after is the shapes become, like, symbols — you know, things. An animal, a chair, et cetera.

The good side is: if you decide that the process is the art. We'll make a gold, sort of ornate frame, and that goes around that whole, you know, weird mechanism with the squeegee and the vacuum and everything. And it gets, like — boom, stamped on. It's like, yeah, see, that's where the art is.

Now we're zooming out. The idea being, like: that was an example of this larger idea. And the larger idea is that the question is, where do you crop art? And this actually is applicable in various situations.

It's going to end with my checkout counter sculpture, where I basically say: well, if I intentionally want to make a sculpture, then you can have this little time period where the sculpture exists, of all the things I picked out. You don't know if I picked them out in order to stack them and make pretty colors and shapes, or whether I actually want to eat them. You know?

Now we're gonna do sort of, like, a little recap summary. We're gonna have, like, a big net image that covers the whole pipeline — and now each of the images we already made goes onto the screen, and the net covers it. Okay: now we're taking everything we learned, and we're gonna recap it and summarize it.

We forgot one frame, which would be the person looking at the art in the gallery that Mason made. Either they're scratching their head, or they have, like, a thought bubble with an idea — a meaning. It's like, oh, it means this. Okay, got it. And so then the frame comes around: that person is, like — okay, this is the art. This is where the art lives.

cards.h: He jubilantly burned all his old artwork
cards.body: Like he had solved the key to a puzzle — “archive,” he proclaimed; he didn't know what to do with his finished art. I saw later, in a Facebook post, that my high school art teacher had jubilantly burned all his old artwork when he switched to a more cartoony style.

Art belongs in this strange category of infinite value and depthless uselessness. The power to express what cannot be said with words; the power to sit in your garage rotting till you go back and realize no one's ever even seen your masterpiece. Every doodle is waiting for its debut — to be suddenly recognized for its greatness, propelled to the walls of a museum, traded for a lengthy check from a collector's pocket.

cards.h: Three times they failed to guess
cards.body: A recent night out with friends turned into a heated debate about AI — and eventually into me showing them pictures of my own drawings, and ones that ChatGPT had made. Three times they failed to guess correctly. A lot of people say the images are low quality, and it only makes one kind of art. Unfortunately, these are just the images people know are AI. The others blend seamlessly into the landscape, undetectable by radar.

cards.h: If I wasn’t the best, why compete at all?
cards.body: Around age 20, I gave up my dreams of becoming a painter — because, though I'm not bad, I also just know I'm not the best. There's people who have more raw talent, are better at mixing in colors, more adept at rendering, even more heart in their finished work. More inspiration, more love of beauty. If I wasn't the best, then why compete at all? I told myself.
And I picked things — such esoteric things — that no one would even try to compete with me, much less win.

But a year ago, on a dare from one of those same friends, I took up journaling. I started adding little “diagrams” (as I called them) to the entries, when there were things I could not find the words for.
One day, I endeavored to add little sketches of everything I was grateful for throughout the day. An extra cherry, added to my ice cream. My friend braiding my hair at a party, et cetera.

I was suddenly overwhelmed by the joy I had once felt in art class. Without a plan to share these drawings with anyone, I took such a simple pleasure in being able to express what might have stayed in my head forever. These drawings were for me, just for me. So they didn't have to follow any rules, or live up to anyone's standards.

lessons.title: Astrology — is it stupid, and how it works

cards.body: That's kind of the phrase people use — as above, so below. [[Picture]] a pool being mirrored: shimmering trees and mountains and stuff on the top, and then mirrored in the pool below.
First of all, everyone knows that there aren't just twelve personalities. So that's important.
[[Sometimes it isn't his sign. Sometimes you threw spaghetti down your shirt and stormed out.]]

Currently, astrology actually is stupid — not because it's based on a false premise, but because the way it's done isn't right. And it's so wrong for so many reasons that it's not actually matching anything.

cards.h: If you actually understand it, it’s not stupid
cards.body: People are complicating things because no one actually understands it. And that could actually be the hook: okay, it's stupid for this and this and this reason — but if you actually understand it, then it's not stupid.

cards.h: Signs and houses are two wheels
cards.body: Signs and houses are two wheels. They should both have twelve, sort of staggered rather than lined up perfectly, so that it's clear they can spin.
We definitely wanna bring in the earth and the sun fact, because everyone already knows that. It's the same as what I already know: the earth rotates every day…
…and the earth also rotates around the sun. So two rotations. And I bet those are matching.
[[The instant you were born, the wheels lock in place. That frozen sky is your chart.]]
[[Your famous “sign” is only where the sun sat. The moon, Mars, Venus and the rest each had a spot too.]]
[[Draw the lines between them. Some angles sit easy, some pull tight with tension.]]
[[A planet looks like it slips backward because we pass it on the inside lane.]]
[[Long before horoscopes, scholars charted the stars by lamplight. The impulse is ancient.]]
Basically: the place where we are in the rotation around the sun gets matched up with a particular aspect of our life, to decide how it's going.

I must admit, this revelation came from those special fungi that one day decided to take me on a road trip. All expenses paid. I say “they decided” because of the unique way that I procured the mushrooms.

cards.h: There I found a bobby pin
cards.body: One day, I was sitting on the toilet in my seven-bedroom loft when I had the urge to reach behind the seat. There I found a bobby pin.

cards.h: It opened on the first try
cards.body: As though I were already on some substance, I felt compelled to use the bobby pin to open the door of my roommate, Nathan, who had gone on vacation, and had left his room locked in his absence. I had never picked a lock or thought to do so — but the door opened on the first try.

And then, without knowing what was in it, or what I was looking for, I opened the top-left drawer of his dresser and took out a little bag of mushrooms. ([[Her footnote:]] he actually didn't mind me taking the mushrooms, when I told him — and even gave me the rest of the bag.)
I call this strange phenomenon instrumentalism. You follow your heart's desire, and it leads you on a path that you didn't know existed.

In the spirit of scientism, I even hatched a neat little explanation for how this works: your mind keeps track of patterns throughout the day, and puts them together into these little urges, and you're led on some quest that takes you to a place you didn't know existed. If this were true, the brain really would be as remarkable an apparatus as they say.

But Jesus told me otherwise. According to the book Channeling Jesus, by Tina Louise Spaulding: “our emotions are our navigation system.” For the unsure sort, often bombarded by shoulds, and the target of regret, this itself is a revelation.

The fact that the answer to our unsureness would be found in our own mind, rather than an elaborate system of rules, laws, and suggestions coming from the outside world, goes against the foundations of this worried sort of chatter.

cards.h: As though our errant whims were a secret code
cards.body: Instrumentalism takes these “convictions of the mind” a step further — as though our errant whims were a secret code. Not the collected patterns of an unharnessed subconscious, but instead: the communications of another world, the spirit world, leading us “right into temptation.”

Whether or not this is indeed the case, I like this philosophy, as it allows me to prioritize what I want, and neglect the often stubborn, bullying insistence of those around me. If I need a magical system to stop taking the ill-conceived advice of those around me — then so be it.

cards.h: Suddenly there was a snake in my path
cards.body: I was once in a fight on a hike. We had ceased communication, and I was trying very hard not to say anything, when suddenly there was a snake in my path. I automatically gasped. I had never seen a snake on that trail before. It was like the snake had sensed the venom between us, and taken that opportunity to show itself.

The gasp had broken the silence, and in figuring out what to do about the situation, we forgot the fight. By the time we reached the next vista, we were holding each other as we took in the scenery. Just then, someone's off-leash Labrador came ambling over and nuzzled our backs. It was like nature had sensed the change in our temperaments, and presented a very different animal companion.

cards.h: The cat would not be petted
cards.body: The cat I often saw on my walk to Whole Foods would not be petted by my male companion, and I took that to mean he was not to be trusted.

cards.h: The first time she’d found a dog cute
cards.body: An adorable Yorkshire terrier peeked out hopefully from behind a fence, on a walk with my mom where she was suddenly able to see my perspective. My mom, who doesn't really like dogs, remarked that she found him cute. Indeed, that it was the first time she'd found a dog cute.

cards.h: The dog was expressing what I could not say
cards.body: On the other hand, when my dad was repeatedly, intentionally missing my point of view, a large golden retriever reared up on his hind legs while we were passing, and growled at him. In a moment where I'd normally feel helpless, unsure what to do, I suddenly felt powerful — as though the dog was expressing what I could not say. My dad, of course, did not take kindly to this suggestion. “Incompetent owner, untrained dog.” But the encounter had shaken him a little.

I still have a hard time believing this last encounter. I was at dinner with an ex, and he was midstream, telling one of his usual fancy tales, when a rat — a rat! — ran under the next table. A moment ago, I had been under his spell, thinking, “maybe he's not such a bad guy.” Here was the universe, warning me so clearly and plainly that this man was a liar.

cards.h: Creatures took the shape of what I was feeling
cards.body: From that point on, I started noticing how creatures took the shape of what I was thinking or feeling. I told him of all the other situations where animals had come to my rescue. He was happy to hear about the dog nuzzling our backs, but did not believe in the snake, or the rat.

lessons.title: What’s the Difference Between OCD and Witchcraft?

cards.h: When I was 10, I had OCD
cards.body: When I was 10, I had OCD. I could not shake this dread that something would happen to my mom, and I developed all sorts of strange rituals to prevent this.

cards.h: Just a trick of the brain
cards.body: Finally, I told my parents, and they set up an appointment with Lindsay, a CBT coach. She tried to do CBT with me, but I wasn't really interested. Instead, I asked her if I needed to keep doing the rituals, and she explained that it was just a trick of the brain, and that I could stop. So I stopped. Quit everything cold turkey, and I was fine.

And then, unrelated, I spent the next 10 years battling with my intuition. Often I would get compulsions, urges to do one thing or another. Often I would say to myself, “that's silly,” and hear the voice of my mother, and therapist, and the myriad science articles I'd read about the way your mind can trick you into thinking things. Guilt or shame, no matter what. I thought I'd kicked this habit. Why was it coming back?

cards.h: I wanted to know once and for all
cards.body: And then I'd either do or not do — and often, if I didn't do, something bad would happen. If I did do it, and something good happened, I'd tell myself I got lucky. I spent a lot of time “tracking” the results of that decision, as a sort of science experiment. I wanted to know once and for all.

As a high school junior, I finally found some solace in art. The mindset required for drawing involves careful observation, and a non-judgmental attitude. All lines are good lines, as long as they accurately describe what you're looking at. This meant that the outcome of a situation was neither good nor bad, just “interesting,” so long as it was observed closely.

At 19, I had dropped out of college to pursue my passion of selling odd commodities. The only one that took off and started making money was the “secretly a witch kit.” People were not buying it ironically. I found myself the head of a witchcraft corporation, a driveway full of crystals, and answering questions like, “how do I do a love spell?” I had 500 decks of coloring tarot cards. Meanwhile, I had never even tried to do a reading — not even for fun.

cards.h: The irony had doubled in on itself
cards.body: The irony had doubled in on itself. I was pretending to be a witch, pretending not to be a witch. I might've accused myself of fraud, were it not for the fact that I knew, deep down, that if anyone had magical powers, it was me.

cards.h: I needed this anger to dissolve
cards.body: Then in 2025, I left a relationship with so much anger that I could barely see straight. The anger followed me around for months while I stayed home and stewed about the situation. My “any outcome is a good outcome, as long as it's carefully observed” mantra was breaking down. I needed this anger to dissolve.

cards.h: I had cast my first spell
cards.body: Until one day it came to me, in bed, trying to fall asleep: just the feeling, without the never-ending current of deplorable actions — betrayal, malice, indifference. And along with it, an image: large black pins sticking straight into his stomach. I concentrated on this image, feeling the white-hot anger bubbling inside me. And then it was done. I had cast my first spell. “If this really works, I need to see the result,” I added as an afterthought. In truth, I did not want to see him harmed — only to see my own anger leave me. I could not think of another way.

cards.h: He came knocking at my door
cards.body: And he came knocking at my door a few days later. He had stomach pain, he said; I needed to forgive him. “I was causing it,” he said. Somehow he knew this — though he was a staunch atheist and believed strictly in scientism. It came back to me all at once, in the car driving to San Francisco. “That's pretty cool,” I thought to myself, when I made the connection. Right then and there, I tried it again: my mom had been complaining about her blurry vision, and I sent some healing her way.

lessons.title: God Only Works in Mysterious Ways

cards.h: The exact thing we asked for
cards.body: Perhaps you’ve heard the adage: “god works in mysterious ways.” Perhaps you’ve even thought to yourself, “yeah, that’s true — cause of this time… I wasn’t expecting that… and then…” However, have you ever thought that God only works in mysterious ways? When we receive our miracle — the exact thing we asked for, delivered in some form that we would never have thought possible, when we least expected it, and in such a way that changed the way that we thought about the circumstances causing us to want that in the first place — we are so mystified, so grateful, so sure that this is the answer to our prayer.

cards.h: They sing to us with significance
cards.body: When we connect the dots of the constellation, they sing to us with significance, and we know somehow, that to question the method of delivery would be itself hubris.

Then time passes, and this sudden, shining moment is like a beacon in our past, whose light fades ever so slightly until one day we dredge up the circumstances surrounding the miracle looking for solace or inspiration in a time of weakness or doubt…

…and find only: scattered stars! No light line connecting them, making the perfect picture we saw before. Each now ordinary star bears the eerie resemblance to a common coincidence! What is it that happened to our brilliant constellation?! We try to reconnect the pieces of the puzzle to see the bigger picture that was so clear to us at one time, but we are left with only crumbling stardust in our hands.
How foolish were we to see these ordinary, most ordinary circumstances, and imagine that someone bigger than us had a plan! Now, we trudge along, our pockets laden with doubt and fear.

And what if this oscillation, which occurs not once, but many times throughout the course of our life, was not a mistake, but by design? I call this: the warp, and the weft. Weaving is mostly a lost craft, but it works by what, when I first discovered it, felt like magic. By a simple mechanism of going under and over every other string and then doing the opposite for the second set of strings, we can create a cloth.

Rather than individually differentiating each string every time, you can insert what is called a “shuttle”: a thin piece of wood, on either end, that automatically differentiates the strings, pulling them apart, and creating a space for the weaving thread to go through. In this way is our faith designed to be. What I find magical about weaving is that the two states coexist together, and without the use of the shuttle, the strings appear uniformly with no differentiation. So is it strange that the world of spirit could coexist so peacefully alongside the world of the physical?

cards.h: We learn to carry an inner light
cards.body: Were it not for the utter and complete blackness with which we are left when we disconnect the string, and are left with just stars, we would have no reason to grope carefully about in the dark, clinging to whatever landmarks we might remember. It is in this way that we learn to carry an inner light. And so to recover the thesis: it is for the sake of this warp and this weft, that god only works in mysterious ways.

At its core is the idea that we're relearning things that we should already have known — that are obvious. And to make it funny, I labeled it an actual disorder. So we can start by making it sound like it's an actual disorder. Which, obviously, it's not.
For example, grounding is basically just walking without our shoes on. We give things complicated names and fancy brand labels when we could just not have changed the thing in the first place.
Pre-peeled bananas — [[that one]] is a metaphor.

cards.h: Those special lamps that have sunlight
cards.body: Also those, like, special lamps that have sunlight. Although those are actually useful, depending on where you live. I guess the picture would only work if the sun was actually shining outside your window, but you were inside with the lamp.

cards.h: A treadmill, watching a nature program
cards.body: I think a treadmill — especially a treadmill if you're watching TV, especially a treadmill if you're watching a nature program on TV — is funny. Because people used to just walk to get food, et cetera. All their basic needs.

cards.h: Even though we’re doing more, we don’t have more time
cards.body: And so this is the bridge: somehow, even though we're doing more stuff, we don't have more time.

cards.h: We’ve extracted the essence of everything
cards.body: I think the reason is because we've extracted the essence of everything, almost like a pill. And this one is sort of a metaphor and an example: instead of eating real food or good food, we just take vitamins and eat crappy food, like McDonald's.
[[Sugar is the essence of fruit; the highlight reel, of a life. Distilled, it leaves you emptier, wanting more.]]

And the funny part is that the people who actually do remember this stuff are then hailed as heroes. There's also sort of a bougie social class thing with it — like, oh, I'm better than everyone because I go outside and touch the dirt. But they write books about it.

cards.h: A treadmill with a doughnut over our head
cards.body: And then the mechanism. This is the part that's actually behind it, and it's a little bit too deep for mainstream audiences, but I wanna include it anyway. It starts a really long time ago: basically, we thought that solving our problems would fix everything. Every day we were walking around, like, I'm hungry, or I'm a little cold. We wanted these issues solved. And eventually, we did — we solved almost all our problems. But really, we're trapped in this weird matrix where we're trying to go somewhere. We're kind of on a treadmill with, like, a doughnut hanging over our head.

cards.h: Solving our problems doesn’t solve our problems
cards.body: We keep trying to get somewhere. But the real fix is to notice our issues with desire, and how solving our problems don't actually solve our problems — because we just keep wanting more things.

lessons.title: For the Hate of the Game
lessons.short: For the Hate of the Game

cards.body: I’ve heard it said that there is “a veil of forgetfulness” that has been placed over earth; that we may live our daily lives, and forget the soul that we are, and the home that we come from. Sometimes, looking up at the sky in the deep dark, on a starry night, the veil is temporarily lifted, and we remember from whence we came. A feeling of peace rises from within, and we are connected to everything.

Try as we might to keep this feeling with us, inevitably it fades like throwing small tinder on a disappearing fire and we go back to the humdrum — the daily wanderings to and fro from errand to market and back again.

In 2012, my second attempt at college was failing. I had caught too many whiffs of this feeling. That magical place, where your soul is in line with the universe, had caught me like the wind, and I found myself on these strange little adventures, where one thing led to another, led to another, and suddenly I found myself in a living room across town, saying grace with a gathering of homeless people. Perhaps stranger, was taking notes in class the next day, wondering what adventures I was missing.

So when I left school and moved to Brooklyn “on a whim,” one stormy night, I was sorely disappointed that whimsy was in short supply when you sought it out instead of waiting for it to happen. My seven roommates, brought together by odd circumstances like the characters in a sitcom, should’ve been the perfect crew for these errands of whimsy, and yet every night we found ourselves passing a joint around in our permanently furniture-less loft.

cards.h: The law was lack of doubt
cards.body: But one day, this most mysterious magic overtook me once again — I played Deer Hunter, and stayed up till 6 with some men I never saw again. What followed was the strangest series of coincidences that I dare not reveal, lest the reader begins to doubt the validity of my account. I now began to engage in these strange mishaps, always a lesson in being carried by the wind, as though they were my full time job. The law of these missions was lack of doubt. No sooner had I to think, “I know where this is going,” and the whole series of steps would change its course.

But if I could leap without looking for long enough, my feet permanently suspended on a cloud of faith, then there was always, what I hesitate to call a prize, waiting for me at the end. As though it were law, I kept nothing from these adventures — not money, not friendships. If numbers were exchanged, they were never called. So it was more like a volley — to see how long I could keep the adventure going, because the longer the ball was in the air, the more hearts and lives I would be given express access to. But try to grab a hold of one of those dangling pieces of gold, and as sure as time, you’d be ejected from the craft.

As time went on, I was scarcely a person, but rather a shape shifter to whatever the game required. I learned that to agree with whatever strange understanding of the world my companions seemed to believe, I would be rewarded. Nod along, and you have won half the battle. And if they should say something that disagrees sincerely with your fundamental understanding of reality, that causes your fingers almost to shake with the effort of not correcting them, then you know that this is the final test, and that sooner or later, you’ll be on to the next level.

I was now able to play the game mostly by its rules. I had learned the patterns that “coincidences” take, and could play the game what I might like to call “blind.” That is: I was no longer even within the chess piece that moved to and fro, but instead, somewhere above, observing the whole picture, strategizing my next move, which was almost always to “do nothing,” and at that, from a considerable distance. A video game that I often lost, but sometimes won, if my heart was in the right place, and I could detach myself from my own heart’s desire long enough to play the game. And so, this is how I learned the rules of a game no one else seemed to know about.

cards.h: I grew to hate the game
cards.body: I grew to hate the game. I would find myself on the balcony of some stranger’s house, some guy with long hair confessing a secret he’d kept for forever. And I would see bubbles floating down in the wind, and know that, were I to climb the dusty set of stairs to the roof, I would find four coworkers at a construction company, about to make a toast, but somehow also happy for me to join them. Strangely, though, what I wanted most was just to go home. Perhaps to get to the roof, and find only a security guard who would stare me down with a steely eye so that I could trudge home defeated, and think, “what a cruel world,” rather than “omg, life is beautiful, there’s magic waiting in every moment.”

cards.h: They haven’t had their coffee yet
cards.body: I had a roommate who once paid me quite a grand compliment. He said “because you are free, and do whatever you want, it makes everyone around you feel free to do what they want to.” And I found myself thinking an odd thought that I could not tell him, which was that, “I don’t get to do what I want, I have to do what I want, and so I never get to do what I want.” Imagine, if you will, this Tinkerbell-esque persona, a lady with long flowing hair, who seems to be the life of the party. She flits from one place to the next, often uttering some incomprehensible riddle about the magic in everything. Now imagine, if you will, that inside this cloud of a person is a heart that is grumbling that they haven’t had their coffee yet.

lessons.title: What Do You Want to Wake Up To?
lessons.short: What Do You Want to Wake Up To?

cards.body: [[My friend Mason — poet, philosopher, red beard — turns to me in the steam and says it like it’s easy. Just meditate. Empty your mind. But I can’t.]]
[[I close my eyes and I’m not floating in calm. I’m flailing in a ball pit, going under, grabbing for the surface.]]
[[Here’s what my mind does instead.]] Sometimes I have, like, a nice giant big idea[[, and it floats up like a soap bubble off a wand.]]
[[What if I threw a party on a train — each car a different theme? A witchy car, a speakeasy car, a jungle lounge. The bubble fills right up with it.]]
Basically, the idea is that, like, negative thoughts start coming in, and I have to push them back.

cards.h: Push them back with positive thoughts
cards.body: I push them back with, like, positive thoughts. Sometimes cognitive vehicles that might not be true, like: he didn't mean it. Or sometimes just with generally positive thoughts, like: well, that's not that big a deal. Or: it's nice and sunny out. But this can only do so much.
But then sometimes I have, like, a nice giant big idea — and it pops everything.

cards.h: When you go down into your thoughts
cards.body: Basically, when you go down into your thoughts — when you get high — you sort of become aware of more things. And you wanna make sure that when you do, you're in a nice place. Not, like, in a garbage dump.

cards.h: What do you wanna wake up to?
cards.body: The meditation thing is like: what do you wanna wake up to?
[[You can get high by yourself in a dumpster, pinching your nose against the trash.]]

cards.h: We would always go to the beach
cards.body: It reminds me of when I used to, like, smoke weed with my friends in high school, and we would always go to the beach or do something really nice — maybe even climb on the lifeguard tower, or, like, do mushrooms in nature. That was really nice.
[[You stretch, you look around, and it’s junk on the floor — everything gone dingy and gray.]]
[[Or you wake up in a bright room to a plan you made the night before — a walk, an afternoon on the floor with scissors and colored paper, a croissant on a plate.]]
[[Getting quiet only takes you inward. The work is making the inside worth arriving in — a room you’d want to wake up to. Build that first, and the quiet gets easy.]]
Okay, so one time I was hanging out with my friend Josiah.

I just, like, climbed this fence, and then I stole someone’s wallet — I went into a restaurant, and they had the bags in a little area for the employees, so I just stole one of them. And then I didn’t really want it, so I just dumped all the cards out on the lawn. So they could find them eventually, maybe. But I don’t know if they did.

Then I took the train to, like, downtown Portland or something, and on the way there I just [[drank]] a bunch of coffee from a cup I found on the ground. And I don’t normally drink coffee, so it made me really, really hyper.

cards.h: You shouldn’t be in this part of town
cards.body: Someone I saw was just like, you shouldn’t be in this part of town. I was like, oh no, I shouldn’t be in this part of town. And so I just ran across the street — but it was actually, like, a five-lane highway or something.

cards.h: You have to run so fast right now
cards.body: I was like, oh gosh. I almost didn’t make it — I almost got ran over. And literally, I remember, because I did track in high school, I was like: you have to run so fast right now. And I did. I ran fast enough that I didn’t get run over.

But then everybody was around me on the ground, cuz someone said they saw my legs go under the car. And I was like, I don’t think so — I wasn’t in any pain. But I tried to get up, and they wouldn’t let me get up. And this one woman who was really nice, she bent down and she was like, no honey, don’t get up, and she [[gave]] me a hug. And I was like, okay, I guess I won’t get up. Just, like, peer pressured into staying there.

cards.h: I’m not going in an ambulance
cards.body:
Then someone called an ambulance, and I was like, I’m not going in an ambulance. So when I heard the siren, that’s when I just jumped up and ran away from the whole crowd of people, and I jumped over a fence.

Oh — and I had found this silver bracelet on the ground, like, a day before. It was really nice. It had these little shapes, and they were locked together, kind of, and there was little beads on them. [[Remember the bracelet.]]

cards.h: Have you ever rode with a black man before?
cards.body: I didn’t know what to do, really, so I just asked for a ride, and I got in the car with this black guy who decided to give me a ride. And he was like, have you ever rode with a black man before? And I was like, I don’t know. I don’t know where I was trying to go — I think I was trying to go home — but I ended up, like, next to a 7-Eleven.

cards.h: I didn’t really know what to do
cards.body: Then I was hiding in this, like, storage container for some reason, just because I didn’t really know what to do. Then I heard the police coming, and so I started to run away from them — because, I don’t know, it was, like, the police, and I didn’t want to get caught.

And then, because I was running away, they started chasing me, and I ended up jumping over a different fence. It’s actually really hard to get away from them. I was kind of surprised, because, first of all, I didn’t, like, do anything wrong, exactly. Like, I did — but not that they knew about. I was just running away probably because I had too much coffee. I’m really not used to drinking coffee.

So anyway, then I got under this parked car to try to hide from them. But then they were like, we’re gonna release the dogs on you. So I was like, okay, I think I’m just gonna get out from this car — because I didn’t actually do anything wrong, and I don’t really want the dogs to be released on me, and I didn’t want to get bitten by a dog.

So then I came out from under the car, and then they asked me, like, if I had done any drugs that day. They asked me if I did any meth. And I was embarrassed that I just had drank coffee. So I said: yeah, I did meth.

cards.h: Your name isn’t Sophie. It’s Valued Customer.
cards.body: And then they said that I didn’t do anything wrong — so they didn’t know I was running away — and that they were just gonna, like, let me go. But then he asked for my driver’s license, and I didn’t have it, because I don’t know how to drive. All I had was, like, a little debit card that you get, you know, when you lose your debit card and they give you one — and it said VALUED CUSTOMER on it. They had asked my name, and I told them, I was like, it’s Sophie. And then they looked at the card, and they’re like: you lied about your name. Your name isn’t Sophie. It’s Valued Customer. And I was like, what, are you kidding me?

cards.h: We’re gonna arrest you, because you’re being mean to us
cards.body:
Then they asked me for my birthday, and I had already given them the day that I was born, and I was like, you can infer it from the day I was born. And they were like, you have to tell me your birthday. I was like: do you have a low IQ? And then they were like, okay, we’re gonna arrest you. Because you’re being mean to us. This actually happened, okay? No one’s gonna believe me anyway.

I was like, don’t you have to read me my rights? They’re like, no, that’s just in the movies. You can’t believe everything you see in the movies.

Then I was in their car, and I was, like, actually upset, and I started crying. And it was really hot, and I was like, can you roll down the window? He’s like, no. And then he was like, okay, you know what, you’re cute, and you’re white, so I’ll just put in a good word for you, and everything will be fine. Oh yeah — cuz also I told them I stole something. I told them I went to 7-Eleven and stole something, and they were like, yeah, she did.

cards.h: They gave me a mayonnaise sandwich
cards.body: So then I went to jail. And they gave me, like, a mayonnaise sandwich, and I didn’t like it, so I gave it to someone else. And I felt really bad for all the other people there, cuz they were actually going to jail. And they fingerprinted me and took mug shots and stuff.

cards.h: The sun was coming up when I left
cards.body: And then they released me. It was already, like, literally the next day at that point — the sun was coming up when I left. And then I noticed that they stole my silver bracelet. Oh my god. Can you believe that? They, like, collect all your stuff, and then they give it back to you when you get released. And then I noticed that something else was missing that I had collected: a shiny penny.

cards.h: Oh. That’s what happened to my shiny penny.
cards.body: I also had a debit card, and I was like, oh, that’s nice — I guess when they get you out of jail, they give you a debit card, because they’re worried about your well-being, so they want to give you, like, some money. So I went into all these stores, and I tried to spend it on stuff, and every time they’re like, you have, like, nothing on here. You have one cent on [[it]]. And then finally, like, five hours later, I was thinking about it, and I was like: oh. That’s what happened to my shiny penny. They turn all your cash into — they put it all in a debit card.

lessons.title: How to Read People — I. Actions & Intentions

cards.h: Theory of Mind is just the beginning
cards.body: When your mind graduates from age 3 to age 4, you’re suddenly able to recognize that people have different thoughts than you do. This is “Theory of Mind,” according to most, and the learning stops here. Unfortunately, recognizing that they exist is only the first step in learning about other people’s minds. And if you’re not intuitively gifted with a high emotional intelligence quotient, then the world of people and relating to people can be a strange and uncomfortable place. But, here’s the good news: you have other faculties you can rely on. You’re excellent at logic, you’re good at recognizing patterns, and you can use these two skills to reconstitute this intuitive lack.

cards.h: “Why is he still talking about trains?”
cards.body: “I really like trains. My favorite kind of train is a semi-automatic locomotive. It produces enough steam per second to fill an entire building! Can you believe that?! Anyway: what’s your favorite thing about trains?” “I don’t like trains. What is he talking about? Why is he still talking about trains?” This is rather simple. You don’t need advanced theory of mind to know whether they are interested in trains. And, if you’re not sure, just ask: “Hey, are you interested in trains by the way?” “Um, no, not really?” “Oh ok. Well, what are you interested in?” “Lady bugs! I love lady bugs.”

cards.h: What is this person thinking right now?
cards.body: Of course, you can’t always ask. So you have to figure it out with context clues. Hmm, they haven’t spoken in a little while. And they’re fidgeting with their fingers a lot. Oh, and they keep looking away from me — glancing towards the bathroom. Maybe I’ll try changing the topic, and see if they start paying attention… At the beginning, it can seem silly to constantly be asking yourself what the other person is thinking. But eventually, it will become natural, and you will start to do it out of habit.

cards.h: Why did this person do this?
cards.body: Ask yourself: why did this person do this? Believe: every action has an underlying intention or motivation (“we do things for a reason”). Step one — important: intentional or accidental? (Conscious or unconscious?) Ask yourself: did this person do this on purpose, or was it accidental? Ask yourself: what is this person thinking right now?

lessons.title: How to Read People — II. The Pattern Collector

cards.body: They all have something in common. The Pattern Collecting Game — how to play: take out your metaphorical (or literal) pattern collector: a simple old matchbox. Choose a pattern you have been collecting — something you are not sure about — gathering evidence about. It could be whether god exists. Every time you see an example, place a tic tac in the box. Once you have enough examples, try to understand what you’ve been collecting (what do the tic tacs all have in common)? If you can’t remember what each of the tic tacs was about, you can use a matchbook, and write down what happened, or a word or two to remind you of what happened later.

cards.h: “I’ll put it in my pocket and save it for later”
cards.body: Ah! There’s an example of that pattern I was collecting! (I’ll put it in my pocket and save it for later.) Collect this pattern: take note — anytime someone does something that disagrees with your current understanding of who they are as a person. File that away for later, and see if you can find other events that seem related to that action (in that they may stem from the same intention). Note: the word intention is used loosely, to refer to the “reason” behind an action. An intention may be unintentional, or other things.

If you’re on a first date, or hanging out with a new friend for the first time, bring along a pattern collector. The pattern being: things I do not understand. Over the course of the day, fill your box with “things you do not understand” about the other person — actions you cannot connect easily to a matching intention. At the end of the date or day, dump out your boxes, and lay them on the table. See if you and your partner can help each other connect your (and their) actions to intentions. Note: as this exercise involves emotional vulnerability, you may want to take some actions to ensure that this is a safe space. Light a candle, and dim the lights. Say to the other person: “I want to get to know you better. No matter who you are, it is ok. This is a safe space, and I will bring no judgment into this space, nor will I take anything out of this space to judge it later.” Let your partner say this to you. End this ritual by touching hands and making eye contact for a few seconds. Optional: preserve the exercise by tacking the cards up on a cork board, and connecting the related ones through thread (to make “constellations”).

cards.h: Imagine if the game were evidence-based
cards.body: Imagine if the game were evidence-based. Imagine collecting instances of each — times when he (they) did something that made you think they might love you, and times when they showed they might not love you.
Imagine collecting these separate instances into two “match” boxes, to compare them.

cards.h: Arrange your event cards into groups
cards.body: You may want to arrange your event cards into groups based on how you suspect they are related — so actions that you think belong to the same motivation can go next to each other. Your partner may confirm or deny that these events are related. You can choose to say how you think they’re related, or let that be ambiguous. Take turns with this exercise, focusing on one intention or group of events. Feel free to ask clarifying questions of the other person, but give the other person the opportunity to opt out of answering, without feeling that there is an obligation.

When you are satisfied with the arrangements of the events for both of you, write, in a different color, what exactly it is you think connects the events (the underlying intention/motivation/abstraction). Your character traits are the summation of your actions — the abstract concept that emerges, when you connect all of your actions together.
[[Pull too hard on one thread and a person seems to point ten directions at once. The contradictions are real, and they belong to the whole person.]]
[[Follow each contradictory thread back and they all meet at one center — the whole person, too big to sum up.]]

Let your mind put each of the events together, and see what they have in common. You might draw a venn diagram, and see if you can fill out the middle ellipse, and then see if this fits with any of the other ones. Compare them in pairs, in sets of threes, or as a group with one or two missing.

lessons.title: How to Read People — III. Expert Mode

cards.body: Intentions are in the moment, but core beliefs and character traits are forever. If an action connects back to an intention, then what does an intention connect to? In the beginning you can use observations about actions to trace back to singular intentions. However, as you gain access to more information (hanging out with someone more), you can evolve this understanding into a more general understanding about their underlying beliefs and core values. For example: “it’s raining as always” — connects back to, potentially, a negative mindset.

cards.h: A version of the memory constellation game
cards.body: You can discover character traits by playing a version of the memory constellation game, and moving the various actions you’ve collected, around in your mind. Is there something they all have in common, besides being in the same matchbox?

Once in a while, a critical event or realization takes place, so as to set in motion a displacement of past events and to imbue them with a new meaning. This new and surprising event sheds light on the situation in such a way that each and every event which came before it now makes a whole different kind of sense. Take, for example, a detective novel, in which the protagonist finds out one missing (and key) piece of information, which allows him to put everything else into place. Or the various pieces of information that line up when Harry Potter realizes Snape isn’t the bad guy he thinks he is.

The trick to a successful execution of RPM is: the Ambiguous Event; a special kind of event that has two possible interpretations. One interpretation is reserved for the present, while the other is set aside for “the big reveal.” The membrane is the actual event that happened, and the story that you’re telling yourself about it. By itself we can’t determine WHICH of the possible interpretations are true. The circle is always a possible option, while the triangle, square, and oval only exist in SOME of the events.

cards.h: In context, we are able to choose an interpretation
cards.body: In retroactive pattern recognition, we begin with one interpretation of the events, and then, based on later information, gain a new understanding of the event, so that we now have an alternate interpretation of the events. Proactive pattern manipulation stipulates that the action is preset for a delayed-time interpretation. This means we perform the action, and are already aware of both possible interpretations — we intend the delayed “aha moment” that will come at the addition of new information. A common metaphor is the delayed reaction ADHD medication, that is not set to release into your system until a predetermined time (later).

Most of the time, Retroactive Pattern Recognition is unintentional. As new information comes to light, there is no intention of shedding light on past information by the person who reveals it. However — some of the time, this reveal is on purpose. In fact, once you get the hang of it, you can use RPM to your great advantage. The best way to effectively pull off RPM is through careful planning. This means planting seeds knowing you will later give them new light. For example, imagine constantly dashing off from dates unexpectedly. This type of behavior might be disconcerting and off-putting. However, with the help of RPM, you can turn this behavior right around by “accidentally” letting slip that you’ve been dashing off to rescue sick puppies, give toys to starving homeless children, etc. “Now that I’ve gotten to know you better, I understand why you did that thing that I could not place when I first met you.”

cards.h: Keep your conclusion as a theory
cards.body: Ways of approaching the problem (strategies): when I do that, why do I do that — caution: try not to project. Patterns in context — what other events may be related in terms of having the same motivation — have there been other similar situations… Keep your conclusion as a theory.

I’ve been doing an experiment every night for the past week. Just before I fall asleep, cuddled up, almost dreaming, I set my mind on something that I want. Not something that I’ve been praying for, wishing for, hoping for, almost angry that I haven’t gotten it, considering I’ve been trying for so long. But something that sounds nice in the moment, possibly impractical, something that wouldn’t affect my life in any particular way, except that I would have that thing, and I would be happy about it.

I’ve had the same bed for ages, a dark wooden one with all these victorian spikes. My mom won’t let me throw it out because it was her mom’s, and everyone who comes over says, “Oh, I like your bed.” So I know I should keep that bed. But I don’t want to. And on night one I started thinking of a pink satin bed that had those cinched up buttons on the headboard. All shiny and pink. And those buttons! I had no idea how I’d get it. Certainly, I didn’t want to find one on Craigslist and lug it into my house. In my mind, as I drifted off, it just sort of came.

cards.h: Suspiciously like the one I’d been imagining
cards.body: The next day, I forgot about this idle wish, and no one came and delivered a bed frame to my door just because they felt like it. But I did see a white headboard that looked suspiciously like the one I’d been imagining. It had those cinched up buttons; I don’t know what they’re called. I walk down my alley every day, on my way to get coffee. Often, furniture stays there for a long time, but I couldn’t remember this one being there before.

On night two, I thought it might be nice to have a cat. Now, I’m not an animal lover, and I can barely manage to feed myself, much less clean up someone else’s poop. So, I know I should not get a cat. But this night was a little bit cold, and I could imagine how nice it would be to have a little cat, kneading its little paws on my bed, and finally, settling down on my chest, so I could go to sleep a little warmer, and with a little more love.

cards.h: Like I was late to a meeting
cards.body: When I saw the cat the next day, perched on this brick wall, staring at me like I was late to a meeting, I actually got scared. Though I hadn’t thought about it all day, my night vision flashed in my mind, and I felt sure if I’d let it, this cat would’ve followed me home, and I’d be destined to take care of it for the rest of my life. It must have sensed my fear, because it jumped off the wall, and gracefully padded in the other direction, though not before glancing over its shoulder to stare me down.

On night three, I knew it was stupid, but I started fantasizing about being gifted my very own chocolate factory, just for being a good person. The magic of finding a golden ticket, that special bar among so many ordinary ones, lingered into my dreams. By this time, I wasn’t surprised to see that my mom had gone shopping and left 3 full-size chocolate bars unopened on the counter. Well, actually one was opened, revealing a bright silver foil, that looked suspiciously like a golden ticket.

cards.h: Why hadn’t I wished for something bigger?
cards.body: You might think that, having gotten my little wishes at least half-fulfilled three times in a row, I’d have sat down and wished for something bigger. I’d be remiss if I didn’t mention that I’m 33 and still without a life partner. And though I’ve mostly convinced myself that I’m better off single, there’s always a nagging feeling that I might someday find the one, and that I might like to. I remembered that one exceptionally lonely night, a few weeks before, I had thrown in the towel, given up all pretense, and decided, “I could actually use a partner.” I let myself envision this ideal romance, dredging up a vision of a masculine presence in my life, complete with hair, color, eyes and personality. In general, this activity is off-limits to a happy single person, so I felt I was breaking my own rules.

This time it came in the form of a hinge message. A masc lesbian called Claire had left me on read about two months ago. She’d chosen today to finally respond. “I’m not on here a lot, but here’s my number…” In her profile, she looked suspiciously like the person of my dreams. Same haircut and everything. Somehow I hadn’t made the connection between my nighttime request, and this errant message the next day. I made the connection now, however. And it stopped me in my tracks.

Later that day, carrying tea, I went on an evening walk. I passed the house where I had seen that cat. Feeling quite sad and alone, I thought, with a certain homesickness, of the magic that that cat had represented. “That was then, and this is now,” I told myself, feeling desperately forlorn. Just then, I saw another cat. A different cat. It was black, and its narrow body swung as it made its way towards me. Magic was here. Magic was everywhere. It didn’t seem to want me to pet it, instead pushed itself gently into my side, letting me have some of its body heat.

I thought maybe I ought to wish for something bigger. Like a horse. Obviously, a horse would not come galloping up to my alley doorstep. Nor did I think my parents would buy me one. But I might expect to find a horse figurine, dropped in passing. Or a poster of a horse… Later, I received one of the more annoying notification sounds, which is from Alibaba, where I buy things from China in bulk. It was an image message, but it wasn’t a picture of a crystal — instead it was a meme. A horse in an office, and the words said: “always there for you.” It didn’t even really make sense. I’d never shared a personal message with this supplier, much less a comedic back-and-forth. I remembered the horse I had been planning on wishing for before, and then there was nothing to do but sit there and let a couple tears trickle down my face.

lessons.title: In Case You’re Curious (Manifestation, Part II)

cards.body: OK, so, I got a couple “signs from the universe,” and now I’m all high on a cloud. No no no, you best believe I’m a scientist at heart. I’ve extended my experiment, and here are all my findings.

In general, I try to avoid sugar, but that doesn’t mean I don’t think about it. It was only natural that this was at the top of my list of desires when I slipped into theta state. I started imagining something like chocolate cake. But even in my imagination, I could see myself sadly walking past, because of my moratorium on sweets. The only way, I realized, that I would actually get to consume the delicious cake, was if someone literally forced me to. Locked me in a room, said: “Sage, eat this.” That Thursday, our housekeeper, who is more like a family friend, was over. When I stepped onto the rug, she disappeared into the kitchen. She came back with some cinnamon cake, and two forks. “Eat!” she said, handing me the second fork. The way she’d arranged it, our two large red chairs were pushed up right next to the two blue couches. There was no way to get out of the living room now — she was blocking the only exit point.

I got a splinter walking around barefoot and could not get it out. It was on the bottom of my foot, making it kind of hard to walk. I tried soaking it in a pot of warm water, I even went to urgent care. Finally, I just accepted it. It stayed there for weeks! Five, to be exact. Finally, I saw this TikTok video about a “magic drawing salve” that you could put on to draw out splinters. I watched the video three times and that night, I imagined over and over again, the splinter coming loose. It came out the next day.

The next morning, the first thing I saw on YouTube shorts was this guy instructing… You lean your head back and hold your breath. Supposedly it forces your energy up into your crown chakra. I did this and went on a walk, and found myself deliriously happy — it was funny, and I found myself laughing and humming to myself.

I’ve been turning to herbalism, to heal myself, and other people. I have no formal training, so one night, I thought “wouldn’t it be nice if someone just came to my house, and showed me how to do it?” My mom is always having jewelry students over, so it made more sense than I thought. I was on a walk the next day when my mom called me to say a woman had come over to get her necklace repaired, and happened to be an herbalist.

I had four friends over for dinner the other day and I told them I wanted to try manifesting something. We settled on an owl and I instructed them to close their eyes. We all imagined a snowy owl flying menacingly towards us and swooping down. The next day, Jack texted me. “Owl spotted,” he said.

Also, note the candle picture, taken at the dinner party. I bought these eyes to attach to my hats so they could say “my eye is up here,” and left them on the table, and Mary found them and made them into a “biblically accurate angel” when the candle burned down.
